questions.q: What is the IUPAC name of this alkane?

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of a branched alkane: a zig-zag chain with two one-carbon branches.

questions.solution: The longest chain has five carbons (pentane), with methyl groups on carbons 2 and 4 from either end. Two identical groups take the prefix di- and a locant each: 2,4-dimethylpentane. (Every substituent needs its own number, and identical ones are combined with di-, not repeated.)

questions.q: What is the IUPAC name of this compound?

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of a branched chain carrying an OH group, a Cl atom and a one-carbon branch.

questions.solution: The alcohol is the principal group, so it takes the suffix -ol and the lowest number: the chain is numbered from the OH carbon, giving butan-1-ol. The substituents are then on carbons 2 (methyl) and 3 (chloro), written in alphabetical order: 3-chloro-2-methylbutan-1-ol. (Prefixes go in alphabetical order, so chloro comes before methyl.)

questions.q: What is the IUPAC name of this aldehyde?

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of a branched compound with an aldehyde group, CHO, at one end of the chain.

questions.solution: The aldehyde carbon is always carbon 1, so it needs no number. The chain has four carbons (butanal) and the methyl group is on carbon 3: 3-methylbutanal. (Numbering from the other end puts the methyl on carbon 2 but the CHO on carbon 4, which is not allowed.)

questions.q: What is the IUPAC name of this alkene?

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of a branched alkene with one C=C double bond.

questions.solution: The longest chain containing the C=C has four carbons. Number from the end that gives the double bond the lower number: it is between carbons 2 and 3 from either end, so the next rule applies and the methyl group gets the lower number, 2: 2-methylbut-2-ene.

questions.q: What is the IUPAC name of this carboxylic acid?

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of a branched carboxylic acid with a COOH group at one end of the chain.

questions.solution: The COOH carbon is carbon 1. The longest chain including it has four carbons (butanoic acid), and the methyl group is on carbon 2: 2-methylbutanoic acid. (Calling it 2-ethylpropanoic acid misses the longest chain, which runs through the ethyl group.)

questions.q: What is the IUPAC name of this ketone?

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of a branched ketone with a C=O group within the chain.

questions.solution: It is a ketone with a four-carbon chain. Number from the end nearer the C=O, which then gets the lower number: the carbonyl is on carbon 2 and the methyl on carbon 3, so 3-methylbutan-2-one. (The principal group, not the branch, decides the numbering; pentan-2-one is an unbranched isomer.)

questions.q: Ethane-1,2-diol, shown here, is used as antifreeze. What is its empirical formula?

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of ethane-1,2-diol: a two-carbon chain with an OH group on each carbon.

questions.solution: The molecular formula is \(\mathrm{C_{2}H_{6}O_{2}}\): two \(\mathrm{CH_{2}}\) groups and two OH groups. Dividing by 2 gives the simplest whole-number ratio, \(\mathrm{CH_{3}O}\). (Forgetting the hydrogen atoms of the OH groups leads to \(\mathrm{CH_{2}O}\).)

questions.q: Which statement describes a homologous series?

options.A: Compounds with the same functional group and general formula, in which each member differs from the next by \(\mathrm{CH_{2}}\)
options.B: Compounds with the same molecular formula but different structural formulae
options.C: Compounds with the same empirical formula and the same physical properties
options.D: Compounds containing only carbon and hydrogen, joined by single bonds

questions.solution: Members of a homologous series share a functional group and a general formula, differ by \(\mathrm{CH_{2}}\), have similar chemical reactions and show a gradual trend in physical properties. (Same molecular formula, different structure describes structural isomers; carbon and hydrogen with single bonds only describes the alkanes, one series.)

questions.q: How many alkenes, including stereoisomers, have the molecular formula \(\mathrm{C_{5}H_{10}}\)?
questions.solution: Straight chain: pent-1-ene, and pent-2-ene, which has E and Z isomers (3). Branched: 2-methylbut-1-ene, 3-methylbut-1-ene and 2-methylbut-2-ene (3), none with E/Z isomers. Total = 6. (Forgetting that pent-2-ene has two stereoisomers leads to 5.)

questions.q: How many structural isomers have the molecular formula \(\mathrm{C_{5}H_{11}Cl}\)?
questions.solution: On pentane: 1-, 2- and 3-chloropentane (3). On 2-methylbutane: 1-chloro-2-methylbutane, 2-chloro-2-methylbutane, 2-chloro-3-methylbutane and 1-chloro-3-methylbutane (4). On 2,2-dimethylpropane: 1-chloro-2,2-dimethylpropane (1). Total = 8. (Using only the straight chain leads to 3.)

questions.q: Which pair of compounds are chain isomers?
questions.solution: Chain isomers have the same molecular formula but a different carbon skeleton. Butane (straight) and methylpropane (branched) are both \(\mathrm{C_{4}H_{10}}\). (But-1-ene and but-2-ene are position isomers; propanal and propanone are functional group isomers; E and Z are stereoisomers.)

questions.q: Which compound is a functional group isomer of the compound shown?

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of propanal: a three-carbon chain ending in an aldehyde group, CHO.

questions.solution: Propanal is \(\mathrm{C_{3}H_{6}O}\), an aldehyde. Propanone, \(\mathrm{CH_{3}COCH_{3}}\), is also \(\mathrm{C_{3}H_{6}O}\) but is a ketone: the same molecular formula with a different functional group. (Propan-1-ol is \(\mathrm{C_{3}H_{8}O}\), propanoic acid \(\mathrm{C_{3}H_{6}O_{2}}\) and butanal \(\mathrm{C_{4}H_{8}O}\), so they are not isomers of propanal.)

questions.q: What is the full name, including E or Z, of the compound shown?

figure.alt: Displayed formula around a C=C double bond. The left carbon carries Cl above and CH3 below; the right carbon carries CH2CH3 above and H below.

questions.solution: The chain is \(\mathrm{CH_{3}C(Cl){=}CHCH_{2}CH_{3}}\): 2-chloropent-2-ene. On the left carbon, Cl (atomic number 17) outranks C; on the right carbon, \(\mathrm{CH_{2}CH_{3}}\) outranks H. Both higher-priority groups are on the same side (above), so it is Z. (Comparing the two carbon chains, which are on opposite sides, wrongly leads to E.)

questions.q: Which compound shows E/Z isomerism?
questions.solution: E/Z isomerism needs two different groups on each carbon of the C=C. In pent-2-ene one carbon has H and \(\mathrm{CH_{3}}\), the other H and \(\mathrm{C_{2}H_{5}}\). Pent-1-ene has two H atoms on carbon 1, 2-methylbut-2-ene has two \(\mathrm{CH_{3}}\) groups on carbon 2, and 1,1-dichloropropene has two Cl atoms on carbon 1.

questions.q: Why can alkenes show E/Z isomerism when alkanes cannot?

options.A: A C=C double bond is weaker than a C–C single bond, so it can twist into two shapes.
options.B: Alkenes contain a carbon atom bonded to four different groups.
options.C: Alkenes have a different general formula from alkanes.
options.D: Rotation about a C=C double bond is restricted, so groups stay fixed on one side or the other.

questions.solution: The π bond above and below the C=C prevents rotation, so groups on each carbon are locked on the same side (Z) or opposite sides (E). Rotation is free about a C–C single bond. (A carbon with four different groups gives optical isomerism, not E/Z.)

questions.q: How is this reaction classified?

figure.alt: 2-Bromopropane is heated with potassium hydroxide in ethanol to give propene.

questions.solution: A small molecule, HBr, is removed from 2-bromopropane and a C=C double bond forms: \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CHBrCH_{3} \rightarrow CH_{2}{=}CHCH_{3} + HBr}\). That is elimination. (With aqueous hydroxide instead, substitution would give propan-2-ol.)

questions.q: Which type of reaction is shown?

figure.alt: Ethyl ethanoate reacts with water, heated with an acid catalyst, to give ethanoic acid and ethanol.

questions.solution: A bond in the ester is broken by reaction with water, giving the acid and the alcohol: hydrolysis. (No small molecule is removed to make a double bond, and no oxygen is added to carbon.)

questions.q: In an organic reaction mechanism, what does a curly arrow show?

options.A: The movement of a single electron
options.B: The movement of an atom from one molecule to another
options.C: The movement of a pair of electrons

questions.solution: A curly arrow shows a pair of electrons moving. It starts at a lone pair or a covalent bond and ends where the new bond or lone pair forms. (A single electron is shown by a fish-hook arrow, with half a head.)

questions.q: In this mechanism step, what does the curly arrow that starts at the C–Br bond show?

figure.alt: Mechanism step: a lone pair on a hydroxide ion has a curly arrow to the δ+ carbon of bromoethane; a second curly arrow starts at the C–Br bond and ends at the δ− bromine. An arrow leads to ethanol and a bromide ion.

options.A: One electron of the C–Br bond moves to the bromine atom, forming a bromine radical.
options.B: Both electrons of the C–Br bond move to the bromine atom, which leaves as a bromide ion.
options.C: Both electrons of the C–Br bond move to the carbon atom.
options.D: A lone pair on the bromine atom forms a new bond to the carbon atom.

questions.solution: The arrow starts at the bond and ends at bromine, so the bonding pair moves to bromine: heterolytic fission, giving \(\mathrm{Br^{-}}\). Bromine is more electronegative (\(\delta-\)), so it takes both electrons. (A single electron would be shown by a fish-hook arrow.)

questions.q: What is the molecular formula of the compound shown?

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of a six-membered carbon ring with an OH group on one carbon.

questions.solution: Six ring carbons: five \(\mathrm{CH_{2}}\) groups (10 H) and one CH bonded to OH (1 H), plus the H of the OH group: 12 H. So the formula is \(\mathrm{C_{6}H_{12}O}\) (cyclohexanol). (Forgetting the hydrogen on the oxygen leads to \(\mathrm{C_{6}H_{11}O}\).)
